title: 5 AI Prompts To Fix Your Entire Life In 1 Day
author: Sandeep Swadia
summary: Argues that AI is useful for self-knowledge not because it has insight, but because your own mind is not neutral — once you find a story that protects you, you stop asking the harder question, and a third party can hold the evidence you cannot. Structures this as five blind spots (deception, relationship, identity, forks, trials) with a specific prompt for each, casting AI in a different role each time: investigator, counterparty, mapmaker, simulator, debrief partner. Every prompt shares the same spine — interview me one question at a time, use only my answers as evidence, and do not flatter me. He is unusually explicit about the limits: treat output as hypothesis not diagnosis, AI is not a therapist, and it cannot know the emotional cost of what you leave behind.
takeaways: The unifying prompt pattern: assign a role, give real detail, then 'interview me one question at a time', use only my answers as evidence, and 'do not flatter me... do not suck up to me'. He repeats the anti-flattery instruction deliberately.
Blind spot 1, deception — AI as investigator. Your life is the black box; crash investigators start with recorded data, not the pilot's memory, because memory distorts under pressure.

Blind spot 2, relationship — AI as counterparty, arguing the other person's case as they would. Eli Finkel's Northwestern study of 120 declining married couples: those who wrote about their worst fights from a neutral outsider's view for ~20 minutes stopped declining; the rest kept sliding.
Every communication has four parts that can differ: what you meant, what came out, what they heard, what they interpreted.

Replace accusation with observation: name the behaviour, name the impact, then ask a genuine question. His example — 'When I don't hear back from you for 2 days, I start wondering if this is important to you. Is that fair?' — instead of 'you don't care about me'.

Blind spot 3, identity — AI as mapmaker. The 'end of history illusion': 19,000 people aged 18-68 could see how much they had changed, but assumed they would not change further. Athletes fused to their sport struggle most at retirement.
Blind spot 4, forks — AI as simulator running Gary Klein's pre-mortem on each option independently, imagining it is two years later and the choice failed badly, then working backwards.
Bezos's rule for acting on it: two-way doors are reversible so move fast; one-way doors are rare and irreversible so slow down.
Blind spot 5, trials — AI as debrief partner. A UT Austin researcher found people who wrote about a painful experience for 15 minutes on four consecutive days were measurably healthier months later.

Feedback beats introspection: a Frontiers in Psychology study found concrete negative feedback reduces self-deception — from someone who knows you, not from strangers online. He keeps a written list of every hard piece of feedback he has received and rereads it.

He names a distinct limit per blind spot rather than one blanket caveat: output is hypothesis not diagnosis; AI cannot know the emotional cost of what you leave behind; it cannot choose the road; and it is not a therapist — for grief you cannot lift alone, use a person.
quotes: Treat the answer as a hypothesis, not a diagnosis. AI is not a trained psychologist. So, why use it at all? Because your own mind is not neutral, either.

Because in every conversation, we bring a story... And too often, the goal of that conversation is to reaffirm that story that's playing in our head... the distance between a conversation and a prosecution is so tiny.
They were just clothes that I was wearing, not my skin. I wore them when it was time, I took them off... The confusion feels existential, but it's just navigational.
AI can help you unpack the story, but you still have to face that person yourself in that room.
You're not asking AI to choose the road for you. It cannot. No one can. But AI can pressure test your assumptions.
AI won't know the emotional cost of whatever you're leaving behind to become someone new. It will make this reinvention of your identity sound crisp and clean. But, life is usually pretty messy.
Pain is what happened. Suffering is the story we keep telling ourselves after... First, there's pain. Then there's music.
bestIdeas: Anti-sycophancy as a prompt requirement. 'Do not flatter me, do not suck up to me' is stated in every prompt because agreeable output is the default failure mode — worth adding to any prompt where you want a real answer.

Interview one question at a time, using only my answers as evidence. Forces the model to build from your actual situation rather than generating plausible generic advice, and transfers to any elicitation task.

Argue the counterparty's case, not mine. Deliberately using a model against your own framing is the steelman move made operational — and the same pattern works on a design or a business case, not just a conflict.

Independent pre-mortems per option. Running each road's failure separately shows how they fail differently, which is more useful than a single risk list. Directly applicable to architecture and vendor decisions.
Roles are clothes, not skin. Holding identity loosely against work is what makes reinvention navigational rather than existential.

Name the limit at the point of use, not once at the end. Pairing each technique with the specific thing it cannot do is a more honest pattern than a blanket disclaimer, and worth copying in any capability write-up.
tools: ChatGPT and Claude — named as the assistants the prompts are written for.
Voice mode — recommended specifically for the relationship prompt, so you rehearse the conversation aloud.
Pre-mortem (Gary Klein) — the decision technique behind the fourth prompt.
Expressive writing — the UT Austin protocol, 15 minutes across four days.
method: 1. DECEPTION, AI as investigator: 'Act as an investigator for my behavior. This is the pattern I keep repeating: [pattern].' Ask for where the blind spots are, why you avoid them, and how to catch them before they trigger. 'Interview me one question at a time... Use only my answer as evidence... give me your best hypotheses, the evidence behind it, and the evidence that's still missing. Be respectful, candid, and direct. Do not motivate me or flatter me.'

2. RELATIONSHIP, AI as counterparty: 'Act as the person I am in conflict with... Do not pretend that you know their inner life.' Give the situation and what you plan to say. 'Do not take my side. Argue their case as they might, assuming they're smart and fair.' Ask what they feel that you are not seeing, the weakest part of your argument, and what they need to hear. 'Help me rehearse the actual conversation.'

3. IDENTITY, AI as mapmaker: 'Act as my transformation partner. You are my mapmaker.' Give where you are and where you are going. Interview to find the gap, then answer five questions: which strengths carry over, which become liabilities, what to leave behind though it worked before, what you have never built but now need, and what to test for 30 days before committing. 'Do not give me abstract purpose advice... Do not give me a 10-year life plan.'

4. FORKS, AI as simulator: 'Act as my decision simulator. I am facing a fork ahead.' Give options and constraints. Run a separate pre-mortem on each: imagine it is two years later and that choice failed badly, work backward. For each road give the most likely failure, the warning signs you would see first, and the cost you cannot reverse. 'Do not tell me what to choose.'

5. TRIALS, AI as debrief partner: 'Act as a debrief partner for something difficult that I have gone through.' Give what happened and the story you have been telling yourself. 'Do not comfort me or try to find a solution.' Then separate the facts, the meaning you attribute that is not in the facts, what was yours to control and what was not, and one thing to carry forward and one to leave behind.

keyMessage: AI is worth using on yourself not because it has insight but because your own mind is not neutral — so cast it in a role that holds the evidence against your story, and keep judgment, and the actual conversation, with you.
